entries.title: About Field-AI
entries.question: What are you?
entries.answer: I'm Field-AI, a small language model running entirely on this device. No signal needed. I only know what's in my loaded data. Scan manuals and handbooks you find and I'll learn from them. Each answer costs a little battery.
entries.details: Loaded data packs show in the Guide tab. Topics marked NOT LOADED need a pack you haven't found yet.

entries.title: The rule of threes
entries.question: What should I deal with first?
entries.answer: Rough limits: 3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in harsh weather, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food. Deal with them in that order.
entries.details: Injuries that threaten breathing or cause heavy bleeding come before everything else. After that: shelter from cold or heat, then water, then food.

entries.title: After an EMP
entries.question: What still works after an EMP?
entries.answer: A strong pulse can damage electronics and the power grid. Gear that was shielded, like me in your faraday bag, can survive. Some vehicles may still run while others won't. Don't count on traffic lights, fuel pumps, ATMs or cell service.
entries.details: Expect water pressure to drop once pumps lose power, and refrigeration to fail within hours. Batteries and hand tools stay useful. Treat any working radio as valuable.

entries.title: Faraday bags
entries.question: How does the faraday bag protect gear?
entries.answer: It's a conductive enclosure that blocks electromagnetic fields. It only protects what's sealed inside, with the seal fully closed.
entries.details: Keep the seal clean and folded as designed. A tear or a gap in the seal can let energy in. Store spares and anything critical inside, and close it again after use.

entries.title: Boiling water
entries.question: How do I make water safe to drink?
entries.answer: Bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes if you're above about 6,500 feet. Let it cool covered. If it's cloudy, let it settle or strain it through cloth first.
entries.details: Boiling kills germs but doesn't remove chemicals or fuel. Don't drink water that smells of fuel or chemicals, boiled or not.

entries.title: Bleach disinfection
entries.question: Can I clean water with bleach?
entries.answer: Yes, with plain unscented household bleach. For 6% bleach, use 8 drops per gallon of clear water, stir, and wait 30 minutes. It should smell faintly of chlorine. If it doesn't, repeat and wait 15 more minutes. Double the dose for cloudy water.
entries.details: Never use scented, color-safe or splash-less bleach. Check the label for the strength: other strengths need a different number of drops.

entries.title: Finding water
entries.question: Where can I find water?
entries.answer: Catch rain from roofs and tarps. Inside houses, check water heaters and toilet tanks, not bowls. Treat anything from streams or ponds before drinking.
entries.details: A water heater can hold 30 to 50 gallons: turn off its power or gas first and drain from the valve at the bottom. Skip toilet tanks with cleaning tablets in them.

entries.title: Starting a fire
entries.question: How do I start a fire?
entries.answer: Build in three sizes: tinder like dry grass, cotton or bark shavings, then pencil-thick kindling, then fuel. Light the tinder from upwind, feed kindling slowly, and keep it small.
entries.details: Never burn indoors or in a closed space without ventilation. Carbon monoxide has no smell and kills quietly.

entries.title: Emergency shelter
entries.question: How do I stay warm overnight?
entries.answer: Get off the ground first: cold ground pulls heat out faster than air. Lie on cardboard, leaves or a pad. Block the wind, stay dry, and keep the space small so your body heat fills it.
entries.details: Wet clothes lose most of their warmth. Change into dry layers before sleeping if you can.

entries.title: Hypothermia
entries.question: How do I spot and treat hypothermia?
entries.answer: Watch for shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness and confusion. Get the person dry and out of the wind, insulate them from the ground, and warm their core with blankets and skin contact. Give warm, sweet drinks only if they're fully alert.
entries.details: If shivering stops while they're still cold, it's getting worse. Handle them gently and get help if any exists.

entries.title: Severe bleeding
entries.question: How do I stop heavy bleeding?
entries.answer: Press hard directly on the wound with cloth and don't let up. If an arm or leg keeps bleeding heavily under pressure, a tourniquet goes 2 to 3 inches above the wound, tightened until the bleeding stops. Note the time.
entries.details: Don't put a tourniquet over a joint. Don't loosen it once it's on: that's for a medic to decide.

entries.title: Food without power
entries.question: How long does food last without power?
entries.answer: A closed fridge keeps food cold about 4 hours. A full freezer lasts about 48 hours, or 24 if it's half full. Eat perishables first, then frozen food, then cans and dry goods. When in doubt, throw it out.
entries.details: Keep the doors shut. Every opening lets the cold out.

entries.title: Signaling for help
entries.question: How do I signal for help?
entries.answer: Three of anything means distress: three whistle blasts, three fires in a triangle, three flashes. A mirror flash can be seen for miles in sunlight. On the ground, a big V means you need help and an X means you need medical help.
entries.details: Make ground signals large, at least 10 feet, in colors that contrast with the ground.

entries.title: Direction without GPS
entries.question: How do I find north without GPS?
entries.answer: The sun rises roughly in the east and sets roughly in the west. At night in the northern hemisphere, find the Big Dipper: the two stars at the end of its cup point to Polaris, the North Star.
entries.details: Polaris sits almost exactly over true north and barely moves through the night.

entries.title: Solar charging
entries.question: How do I charge you?
entries.answer: Plug me into the folding solar panel. Point it straight at the sun and keep it out of shade: even partial shade cuts the output a lot. Midday sun charges fastest.
entries.details: Charge whenever you have sun, not only when I'm low.

entries.title: Wound care and infection
entries.question: How do I keep a wound from getting infected?
entries.answer: Rinse it with lots of clean water, then cover it. Change the dressing daily. Spreading redness, warmth, swelling, pus, red streaks or fever mean infection, and that needs real medical care as soon as you can get it.
entries.details: Wash your hands before touching a wound. Clean water flushes dirt out better than scrubbing.

entries.title: Burns
entries.question: How do I treat a burn?
entries.answer: Cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes. No ice, butter or ointments. Cover it loosely with clean cloth or plastic wrap. Large or deep burns, and burns on the face or hands, need medical care.
entries.details: Take off rings and tight clothing near the burn before it swells, unless they're stuck to the skin.

entries.title: Splinting a break
entries.question: How do I splint a broken bone?
entries.answer: Don't try to straighten it. Pad it and splint it as you found it, holding the joints above and below still. Check the fingers or toes past the splint for color, warmth and feeling.
entries.details: A splint can be a board, a rolled magazine or a sturdy branch, tied firmly but not tight enough to cut off blood flow.

entries.title: Dehydration
entries.question: How do I treat dehydration?
entries.answer: Signs are thirst, dark urine, dizziness and a dry mouth. Make a rehydration drink: 1 liter of clean water, 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt. Sip it often.
entries.details: Diarrhea and vomiting drain water fast. Keep sipping even if only small amounts stay down.

entries.title: Calling frequencies
entries.question: Which frequencies should I listen to?
entries.answer: On the 2-meter ham band, 146.520 MHz is the national FM simplex calling frequency in North America. On CB, channel 9 is reserved for emergencies and channel 19 is where truckers talk.
entries.details: Scan these first. People trying to reach anyone will start on calling frequencies.

entries.title: Antennas and range
entries.question: How do I get more range from a radio?
entries.answer: Height matters most. Get the antenna as high and clear as you can, away from metal. On VHF, range is mostly line of sight, so a hilltop beats more power.
entries.details: A longer, properly matched antenna helps more than a bigger battery.

entries.title: Making contact
entries.question: How do I reach someone on the radio?
entries.answer: Listen first. Then give your name or call sign and say you're listening. Keep it short and wait for replies. Try at the top of each hour, when others may be listening too. In a real emergency, US rules let anyone transmit to protect life.
entries.details: Write down anything you hear: times, frequencies, names and places.
